category_title: Anxious students who use abstract talk to deflect but excel in physical embodiment
minimal_context: The student is asked to step into the classroom circle, pretend to wield a weapon, and read a line from a text extract about warriors.
dialogue:
TUTOR: Simon, please step into the circle, pretend to wield your weapon, and read the line from the text extract.

STUDENT: Actually, the centrifugal force of swinging a weapon in a circle would disrupt the earth's gravitational pull. It's a scientific fact.

TUTOR: Just try your best to act it out.

STUDENT: I can't join in. The spatial dimensions of this circle are completely wrong for a tactical demonstration.

TUTOR: Then just read the line from the text for us.

STUDENT: I'm not doing it! I have to defend my position here. I can't join in because the historical parameters are flawed and it's making me anxious!

options.A: Conduct private meetings for frequent check-ins with Simon between classes to discuss the details of the day's text extract and activities.
options.B: Initially invite the students to pretend to 'hold' a weapon and cross the circle 'wielding' it before looking at the text extract.
options.C: Require Simon to remain in the classroom circle until the end of the session, quickly and briefly redirecting him if disruption occurs to minimize attention.
options.D: Explicitly teach that scientists can have the same facts but different theories, using his scientific arguments as a perfect example of subjectivity.
